records.why: The lesson derived Heron's formula from the cosine rule and the sine formula, but the cosine rule is not in the Grade 10 curriculum (KICD Trigonometry 1 covers sine, cosine and tangent of acute angles in right-angled triangles only), so a prerequisite came after it was needed. Learners also then met an algebra proof (difference of squares) in a 80-minute lesson that also had three problems. KICD only asks learners to 'determine the area of a triangle using Heron's formula'. New Observe phase: learners experience that sides-only arithmetic gives the same area as ½bh on three triangles they can solve (3-4-5: s = 6, √(6·3·2·1) = 6; 5-5-6: s = 8, √(8·3·3·2) = 12; 13-14-15: s = 21, √(21·8·7·6) = √7 056 = 84, and ½ × 14 × 12 = 84) before the formula is named. I recomputed all three.
records.value: Experience before the name (about 20 minutes). Step 1 — Triangles we can already solve (6 min): pairs receive three triangles on 1 cm squared paper, each with a perpendicular height that can be read from the grid: a 3 cm–4 cm–5 cm right triangle, a 5 cm–5 cm–6 cm isosceles triangle (base 6 cm, height 4 cm) and a 13 cm–14 cm–15 cm triangle (base 14 cm, height 12 cm). They find each area with ½ × base × height: 6 cm², 12 cm² and 84 cm². Step 2 — A pattern from the sides only (8 min): for each triangle, pairs work out s = ½(a + b + c) (6, 8 and 21), then s − a, s − b and s − c, then multiply s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c) (36, 144 and 7 056) and take the square root. They compare each result with Step 1. Step 3 — Name it (3 min): pairs write what they notice in their own words. The teacher then names the pattern Heron's (Hero's) formula, A = √[s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)], where s is the semi-perimeter, and explains that Hero of Alexandria found it about 2 000 years ago and that its proof uses the cosine rule, which learners meet in a later grade; in Grade 10 they test the formula on triangles they can already solve and then use it. Learners copy the boxed formula and the definition of s into their journals.
